Making friends is actually such good advice. I do envy people who made friends and meaningful connections in uni. I'm a 3rd year student and for me that just didn't happen, I am on friendly/neutral terms with everyone, but actively spending time with people there either feels like a tiring duty or doesn't lead anywhere. And it is much much more difficult to study when you feel isolated. For several years i've been doubting if i should've gone for a different major because of that feeling. Last year i joined a big IT community outside of uni (and found several good friends here and there) and suddenly realized that i wasn't the problem. at least, that i love my major and i'm not shit at communication. It just so happened that i didn't match interests/goals/ideals with anybody i met in class and wasn't confident enough to talk to the professors. Believe in magic of friendship, everybody, it changes your life

author: @__sw__1
text:
I am glad I stopped comparing myself after Igcses/Gcses
I see people in my class still argue over who got more marks and hence whos smarter
But really who cares everyone is in their own journey in life, I never thought once a higher grade meant more intelligence it just meant more effort put in and consistency. Sure some people are smart but then again doesn't affect me

The famous saying: "C's get degrees", as an engineer don't be just a book worm who aces grades, you have to be able to make real projects learn by building, enjoy your life don't just chase the grind 24/7 balance is key, end of the day your employer will just see your certificate
this doesn't apply for a levels tho just university in general i think

General Thought, if you're doing engineering then actually utilise your teachers, i guess people go university, skim through assignments with ai then fall into some sort of 50k debt with no plan and never really utilise the fact their professors have PHDS in the topic or the resources or the labs to create and do something on their own. 

When it comes to jobs you just gotta learn the corporate playbook if I am being honest- I haven't been there yet but really gaining connections , learning networking some other skills are just as important as working, market correction pricings for your role etc 

Some Resources
UCAS itself
Reading Lists from top unis(eg oxford reading list, imperial reading list)
MITopencourseware, literally any opencourseware website MOOCS, openlearn
Youtube to learn stuff
Document a project
Unifrog, Unibuddy, prospects and similar websites, take small actions if in doubt to figure out what you want to do currently in that stage
please don't read generic books to be performative just find something that interests you and read about it 
the feynman lectures website volume 1 and all its volumes

video_title: Essential Tech for Engineering Students
author: @aguila17
text:
If you want a Mac, and you need to touch anything even remotely related to CAD, without access to remote desktops, you will need windows, and you’ll need to virtualize it on a Mac, on top of that, it will most likely be a x64 build, so it has to go through a translation layer AND a VM, account for this when getting a Mac. Pro models are adequate, Max models are probably overkill. 24 to 48 gigs of ram is what you should be aiming for. Paying for parallels is worth it, they have a student discount, virtualbox is trash, VMware is alright but sometimes it doesn’t get hardware passthroughs as neatly as parallels. Yes it’s a hassle, it’s another subscription, but it’s worth the money. 

Alternatively if you do have access to properly implemented remote desktops just save the difference and invest it in an external monitor.

video_title: Essential Tech for Engineering Students
author: @hughjanus8450
text: Im a freshmen mechanical engineer and my biggest advice is to spend the extra money (I understand if people can’t afford it) for a laptop with a dedicated gpu especially if you do not have a desktop. I have the Lenovo Yoga 9 Ultra with the RTX  5050 and it has been solid other than a couple of bugs and meh battery life. I also was able to find it on sale for $1600 (Yes it is still a lot of money but compared to other laptops with similar specs it had a lower price). A buddy of mine has essentially the same laptop as me but with an i7 processor but no dedicated GPU and trying to help him CAD projects in Fusion360 with his laptop is so extremely slow. Do not get any Mac for ME unless you want to attempt to run windows then attempt to run programs like Solidworks from that. You’ll end up buying another device. If you do not have any sort of calculator but need something the TI-30XS or the TI-36X pro are solid in my opinion because you are more likely going to be able use them for whatever class compared to like a TI-84 and you can find them for $20ish, but they do not have graphing capabilities.

video_title: Essential Tech for Engineering Students
author: @alexandria1.
text:
I'm currently studying mech E, and something i've noticed is that (I take notes on an iPad 10th gen? with an Apple Pencil) and my friends with ReMarkable's can't put their work onto their desktop, whereas I just have a shortcut configurated that will automatically overwrite a PDF in my google drive with the same file name, but different notes. It's INVALUABLE. I can just click one button and shove the iPad in my backpack, and when i get back to my room, it's a click away from being on my desktop. Makes it really really easy to pull up on my second monitor when I'm studying, so that way I have way more screen real estate (and yes I know this is petty, don't have to crane my neck up and down). I'd strongly recommend an iPad, and just, if you must, put screen time limits on it, with a pin known by like a close friend and not yourself, and use a seperate iCloud if you have an iPhone, so your texts and emails and notifications don't all sync up.}
On that same note, I think a desktop is worthwhile investment. My university does technically have cloud computing, but having everything immediately when I need it is great, and it lets me set up macros and different tiny little optimizations. Plus, most people already have one, so it's just a matter of bringing it to college. 
Laptops are fine, I have a 2008 thinkpad running arch I bought for $50 on facebook marketplace that I use for library studying, but I much prefer my desktop in my room on account of having a single. 
Otherwise, I really appreciate the video, and wish there was more discussion on starting university tech before this year. Cheers!

video_title: Essential Tech for Engineering Students
author: @betaomega04
text:
As someone who has ALL of the tech things, I would try to steer away from E-Ink for taking notes. I completely understand the convenience, but I have to be honest... my paper notes... being able to visually see several pages of notes all at once was absolutely invaluable to me. You can't do that with E-Ink. It was way easier to draw out tables, systems, complex problems, cram little writings here and there. This system was incredibly flexible across my three majors. 

I would use unruled Hammermill 32 lb 100 Brightness computer paper. Every page had a custom header that had the school's symbol, a space to write the class it was for, the date, and the page number for that date, and at the bottom my all my contact information in a single line. Each class had its own 1/2" Heavy Duty Binder with super-heavy page protectors. 

Everyone is different, but I think there is something to the older ways of taking notes.

video_title: It took me 6 years to realize what I am about to tell you in 17 minutes
author: @ivzednem
text:
I think at the end of the day most early career engineers think that it comes down to skill and skill alone. I wasn’t the most skilled in college, but I’ve gotten lucky and landed jobs where I’ve been able to learn significantly and rapidly. I couldn’t have done that without connections and friends that worked in the industry. Three things that have worked for me and have been absolutely huge for my career: 

1. You have to be able to work well with people and understand how to supplement a team. You don’t know everything and you never will.
2. You have to be curious and understand how things work down to the detail. The more hand waving you do the higher the risk your design/test/decisions won’t work. 
3. Grit really is huge despite it being last on my list. Being able to fall down and get back up. IMHO you learn more when things fail because you have to understand why things aren’t working. When things work the first time there might be things that you don’t consider at first. 

If any of this does not stick in terms of what you want to do unfortunately engineering is not for you. I can guarantee this will bleed into other aspects of your life which may be a double edged sword, but these are absolutely crucial to your development in your career. There are also levels in terms of how deep you want to go. That’s up to each person’s discretion. Best wishes to anyone reading this.

author: @meppeorga
text:
One year I sent around a thousand CVs, varied too, software engineering. Also Poland btw. 
Most job interviews offered no feedback for self-improvement honestly.
After a while I scraped some freelancing experience and honestly stopped caring, that's ironically when I landed a position at a big corpo. 
At first I thought it was my dream job, it wasn't, big tech is soulless and stifles what you can do to the point of burnout.
After they fired me (because of an AI investment with no net return) I basically decided to make a gamble and divert my experience into other things and topics I was interested in (I already did so when working there because I knew there would be firings, and obviously people with the least experience get dropped first). 
I dived into hardware topics, linux, administration and electronics.
And it was the best decision I ever made because that got me into a startup making high end speakers, it's a split physical and office work, and it's the best job I ever had and the vast challanges it presents I still welcome with a smile, I can't imagine any other place that would provide me with what this job offers. 
Not to mention it's probably the first time when I really feel that I can really use, expand and retain my knowledge in the field.
If this business ever fails (currently doesn't look like it will anytime soon) I don't really worry because I know I will land another job after this, but I obviously hope it doesn't so I don't have to go back to the world of big tech.

video_title: It took me 6 years to realize what I am about to tell you in 17 minutes
author: @BenjaminvanDijk-b7p
text:
As an RF engineer now, the most important thing I can say is, since so many nowadays roll out of uni with a high level education, it's more important than ever to differentiate yourself outside of university itself. I noticed people who got jobs the easiest were ones who delayed their studies to work part time at local companies fulfilling basic engineering roles and/or people who were continuously building stuff as a hobby at home after school. Grades are unimportant, if you're good at a certain field, you WILL get noticed.

I fairly naturally got my job during my studies, I think i delayed like 4 years but I mostly relied on experience through my hobbies. My GPA sucked ass but at the other hand I got cherry picked and hired to do research resulting in publications to my name before receiving a diploma. After my studies I continued working fulltime for them. 

Its really important to realize that once you commit to the studies, you'll most definitely compete with people where engineering absorbs their entire lives. For me, but definitely all my older colleagues too in industry, engineering is our jobs, our hobbies, our weekend project, it dictates our holidays, you wake up and go to bed with this stuff on your mind, it starts young and it's a term that should make you feel warm and fuzzy inside. 

And ofcourse it is not easy, and ofcourse it involves things you don't want to do. But if it gets at the stage it feels like "suffering", and I've recently seen a spike in videos how "artrocious" engineering studies apperantly are (which, I also really hate doing homework but if you follow your study guide and actually put the recommended hours in you're almost guaranteed to pass) then maybe its a good thing to really reconsider and find something else, or figure out how to rekindle the flame for the field.

Engineering and passion go hand in hand. You'll need every ounce of passion in you to maintain your mental health as its the most unrewarding field to operate in since you change the world but it's exceedingly hidden behind flashy screens and plastic covers.

video_title: It took me 6 years to realize what I am about to tell you in 17 minutes
author: @spika5872
text: I've worked in R&D for 16 years. OT (unpaid), work on weekend, learning new thing, keep trying and find out why something works or don't work. Still think about work at home, can't stop. This is the life as an engineer. You will continue to do this until you retire and probably not retire... I know people are still working like this in thier 60s, 70s and 80s. I never have time to see my friends and family, never have time to feel love or anything. Lost my feeling towards anyone or anything. Just work. This is my life, my personality and my future now. Not like I hate it, but this is the only thing I have now. If you are not prepared to live and die as an engineer, don't become an engineer. There are many opportunities but getting your foot in the door in R&D is difficult. It's not you are bad but because R&D departments / companies look for extremely specific set of skills and they want you to learn fast or, better, don't need much time to pick up the projects the last guy left around. In the old days, companies take in people and train them for years, but I am talking about 50s to early 80s. Yep, it was even way before my time. Nowadays, most companies (if not all) want someone to just start producing results without paying the employee for a few years. Not to mention the person who can help you to pick up the slack is probably overwhelmed by many projects and responsibilities and probably underpaid to deal with you. Each gnerations of new students are harder to get jobs. It all started with the dot com bubble and then the Lehman brothers, and now the several wars (including both Biden and Trump administrations). Things have always been going down hill since decades ago, regardless of who's the president. It's just a matter of how fast we are going downhill. Employess have always prefer experience over degree. I knew it when I was still in undergraduate. I work on project at home and showed them in conference, got an attention from one guy who tried to hire me but in the end didn't but he refered me to another company and that was my 1st job. The boss did not give a damn about my GPA as long as it's above 3.0 and passed Q&A / interview session. The only thing I can advise the kids to do these days is to get intern, get part time or personal project going to show your worth. You need to sell yourself as a product and those are the demo / advertisement to show prospective employers what you are capable of and if your skill set fits their needs. The hard truth is that you realy need to love engineering, if you don't, you would end up working something else. I know 10 people graduated with me and only 3 of them (including myself) are working in engineering after 10 years. Over half of them did not even get an engineering job  to begin with right after graduation. It has always been tough to get a real engineering job even 16 years ago and it's worse now.

JUST A THOUGHT AND A REALLY LONG ONE: hope you read this:
Not to be overly religious on you but we believe you only get what is good for you to get
Nobody else in this world will take a role that was meant for you to take, not even a single penny worth of work

Whenever somethings bad its more so oh it wasn't meant for me, something better is even if I don't know how exactly
Hope you got the message

I am not even in Uni yet, college in the uk but the story of being behind for me is what makes me feel weird , coming in as an international student they usually hold you back an year if you're unlucky which I was. It just gets into your head and you feel you're not good enough or you're not meant for it, and I let the grades I got define me for the longest time. But then just a flick switched and I started just realising hey this all doesn't matter- yes it does in a way but lowkey lifes good what happens if i don't get that fancy title that fancy role, nothing its a luxury it was never something about oh its the end of the world

it was always I 'want' not 'need' this

another thing i realised is we never ever give ourself time to think what we truly want to do with our life
yes its about getting that job that money travelling the world blah blah

but honestly speaking? 
when was the last time you sat down with no stimulus, no music, no tv on, nothing it was just you and your thoughts for 30 minutes
and you just went off that autopilot mode of (work , social media , work work reach the top, work) 

if there's a way to phrase it would be- what would you do if you were in a random mountain in the middle of nowhere with no obligations and you had all the free time in the world?

just overall, give yourself that time of clarity and that time to do other things outside of just chase the sort of autopilot mode that we all are in atm and just you'll feel more present in the moment i guess

text: A few things with NotebookLLM that may cause issues down the line. If you're using it to synthesize information and to see how others can tie into your own work, make sure you actually understand it. You can't fake competence. And using LLMs to sound like you fit in a company's moral framework is bordering on unethical behavior. Every company has, or at least should, have the same core principles. It stems from being a decent human being. Use it if you genuinely want to be a better human bean. If anyone I ever hire fakes a cultural fit and I sense it down the road, I'm keeping a close eye and they're unofficially on thin ice.

video_title: Seriously watch this before you do engineering
author: @benk-kb6db
text: Different world here as someone who got into engineering mainly because I didn't know what I wanted to do and pressure from family… What I really wanted was security and something to go home about. Doing engineering from my experience was really realizing that it wasn't about whether someone was made for engineering it was really about knowing how you can make yourself fit for it. A lot of people that go into engineering come from strong interest in the idea of engineering or have been academics in math and physics which helped pave the path for them and I did not have that. Engineering is hard and will punish you if you don't respect yourself and respect your time and while at times it might make you feel like it is not the right thing for you, it can also show you how far hard work can take you. If all goes well I should graduate next year with my engineering degree and I know when I hold my diploma I would never look back to see that student that always struggled and felt like they fell behind because everyone does and at times its just because they weren't dealt the right cards. The word success would not be definable if we did not have a word to describe what failure was so never let a past mistake or even a past failure stop you from thinking you'd never make it an engineer because you will. Aside of math and physics engineering is all about commitment and effort to prove to yourself that you can go out into this world and do something great and once you struggle through it and eventually graduate you won't see what it took you to get there you would only see greatness one that you've achieved and is truly yours and nothing anyone says or does would ever change that. Point is struggling through it is normal and having those thoughts about wanting to quit or give up will find you but don't let them stop you. Be strong and resilient but also proud of what you've done because not many can say they even attempted engineering and even fewer people can say that they have done it.

video_title: Brutally honest advice for engineering students
author: @bottomethgear9622
text:
You miss something even harsher, idk if you can even handle:

All the "difficult" things you learn in college is NOT the secret sauce. It's your cumulative hands-on experience that you accumulate through experimenting & trying things out.

This also links to privilege. Some parents are supportive enough to buy you circuit boards, arduino, and stuff so you can start from the age of 10, while some parents are too much of a douchebag to not let their kids explore anything else other than tests.

You ace your tests and still mess up at work? Normal. Tests are oversimplified versions of the real world. Overconstrained boundary conditions that will not hold in real applications. You'll sometimes lose against someone from trade school who just has more hours spent hands-on than you.

If you like it, start small. Start early, where there are no consequences of failing. Everyone starts by making scraps.

author: @EllinIsLivid
text:
Thank you, I'm 23 and Gonna start doing Access to HE Engineering in September then go to uni next year. Since aged 7, I wanted to be a surgeon but not to save the world, memorise a million facts or care for the sick — but literally to cut open and optimize the body like a machine. I'm so glad I didn't signup for medical school and all the emotional labour and rote memory. At least you don't have to soothe and reassure the Machine you're trying to fix.

I've always loved maths and science and was the 3rd best at math in my year group in middle/high school. My problem is I feel like engineering is for geniuses. I think of ppl tinkering with cars and you ask "how do you do that, what are you doing, can you teach me?" And they don't even wanna show you, they just ramble on about how easy it is and how you need a steel hand and a good eye etc etc without showing you. So I keep thinking of engineering as this cool thing you can either do or you can't. Genetic birthrights or some deterministic fuckery.

Like Lexi from Emkay, or those kids on Robo competitions.

But they just got exposed early because family likes gears. Who tf even has a circuit board lying around? In modern times, the only time you see a wire is in hazards. It's a privilege to be born to parents who:
1) had cars/spare electronics/circuit boards and 
2) allowed them to explore, not just the adults or the smart older brother

I'm tired of engineering and electronics being gatekept by people who got born lucky. Your videos make it accessible for those who got yelled at for touching things rather than encouraged to get their hands dirty.

video_title: If you're an ambitious engineering student, please watch this.
author: @douglasstrother6584
text:
Knowledge is knowing about something;  skill is the ability to do it well.

"To use mathematics effectively in applications, you need not just knowledge but *skill* .  Skill can only be obtained through practice.", from Mary Boas in "To The Student" of her "Mathematical Methods in the Physical Sciences".

This is true for both applied (computational-oriented) and pure (theorem-proof oriented) courses.  I'm in my 20's (for the third time) and *still* work through the derivations, examples and solve problems to really "get it" when learning new stuff.


A Learning Curve generally looks like a staircase function.

video_title: If you're an ambitious engineering student, please watch this.
author: @douglasstrother6584
text:
We all start from our own "Square One".  One can't know one's capabilities until one makes the *attempt.*

Accomplishment  =  Talent * Effort^Focus  +  Random Events.

*Effort* and *Focus* are in one's control.  Talent is revealed by the application of Effort;  Talent is like a rough ashlar extracted from a quarry whose superfluous parts need to be laboriously chiseled away to expose an exquisite sculpture hidden within.  The second term can take on positive and negative values;  be alert for both the good and bad breaks.

author: @bor_dor
text:
Maybe focusing on one thing is good for a short time, but when it comes to engineering; it is such a broad field that I could end up hurting my progress. There are so many prerequisites and corequisites that it seems almost inevitable that I will gain insight from topics that don't even seem related.
All of the other advice is great, but for me that singular focus is impossible. My mind is constantly jumping from subject to subject, and I have made my peace that I'll always be a master of none. I feel like if I just gain enough fundamentals of most subjects then by the 80/20 rule I'll be able to solve most problems in many various fields. 
I'd rather dig a wide hole than a deep one. But, that's just me. For others, that bit of advice might be exactly what they need, and being a specialist will pay off far better than being a generalist.

video_title: 1st year of electrical engineering in 5min
author: @youtuuba
text:
All those years of college, getting degrees sometimes or at least doing the coursework without petitioning for a degree, in electrical engineering, structural engineering, architecture and music. Seems like a million years ago now. I am sure that of all the things I 'learned' through all of that, I only actually used less than 20% in parallel careers over the decades before retirement. In the electrical field, having basic algebra, trig, fluid dynamics, a good amount of fundamental circuit theory, and a ton of 'rules of thumb' was actually needed and used on a daily basis, the rest vaguely recalled but too fuzzy to be useful. However, AWARENESS of peripheral concepts was crucial to 'figuring out problems' and 'making things work in the real world'.....well, I can't tell you how often little bits and pieces came to mind that ultimately made the difference between success and failure, or being mentally equipped to have the "aha!" moment that saved everything, and that could not have happened if I had not had the early exposure to all that information and concepts.

Structural concepts would suddenly and unexpectedly come in handy when designing a large control panel or even just working on projects around the house. Fluid dynamics allowed me to understand what the mechanical engineers were talking about during project planning meetings. Often, although I had forgotten how to do some abstract thing, at least the concepts and terminology were still there in the back of my brain, allowing me to know WHO to consult with and HOW to explain my problem accurately so they could help. Even those basic chemistry courses, of the kinds required in engineering curriculums, would come in handy in unexpected ways, even if I had forgotten how to solve a reaction.

During my career, I also wrote low-level computer programs for the purposes of testing hardware I had designed (the heavy programming was done by specialists), pretty much ALL of the 8-bit microprocessors, and several high-level languages including BASIC, FORTRAN, C, etc; all learned on my own as I needed it for work projects (I did actually take a semester of BASIC and a semester of FORTAN in college). Then I also learned symbolic logic programming for automation controllers such as PLC's & DCS's, and got to be quite proficient in writing huge and complex applications; all learned on the job. 

But covering ALL the topics described in this video in ONE year, well, I have to assume that was just a quick familiarity pass. Actually studying all of that would be impossible in such a short period of time. A lot of times, students will say they "studied" a topic, when in fact they only had a 'primer'.

video_title: 1st year of electrical engineering in 5min
author: @jbsimmons54
text:
Been an EE for 50 years. Agreed. I see they had to add Algebra to college level as kids couldn’t hack it in high school. We had 2 years of Calculus and a year of Differential Equations, and a semester of Statistics. Magnetism and its calculus was the worst in rotating machines. We had a year of Mechanical Engineering basics and a year of Civil Engineering basics. Computer Science was in extreme infancy as was digital circuits. But we had to pick that up in OJT and continuing education. So I added both Math and Computer Science majors as well to EE. Well rounded education we had. Things are grouped differently today. ALL IT is now under the EE degree, although you can get a degree in those separately. But when it comes to layoffs, those sub degrees are too specialized. A company would never lay off an EE degreed person because their knowledge is _vast_ compared to subspecialty degrees. 

And yes, I wound up working for Intel and IBM in the 80’s. I also was one of the co-inventers of the Quad Core CPU and wrote all the diagnostics for Intel CPUs and PC systems. My first job out of college was with GTE with digital switching telephony systems and that was the nascent internet back then. Frames and frames of discrete digital hardware for CPU, memory, I/O, and networking including all the software. Same for the IBM System 360/370 then. Discrete digital hardware before there were “chips”. What a ride it’s been! Retired now.

author: @tomctutor
text:
I am a tutor and recommend students learn the Units (their use and definitions), dimensional analysis, using tools like Desmos, Wolfram Alpha and being able to use more powerful graphics calculators. Also being able to write up a report on theory of operation, design, testing an electrical circuit as well as using multimeters, digital scopes and fault tracing techniques. Students should try and understand modern power supplies, inverters and other types of power systems and components (triacs, thyristors etc). 
All this helps to bridge the gap between theory in the classroom with context in the real world.

My younger brother was like you. Ask him to fault find, design, or build an electronic circuit and he'd be straight around my place trying to get me to do it. He never kept up with the rapid changes and once he became unemployed couldn't find another position, because at 30 years of age he was competing against younger faster people who would work for less money.
I was taught that theory, but not how it applied to real life. Had to ask a lot of questions to people who were actually using the stuff. It would be more relevant if you started by handling the real things, and then were taught the theory behind how they work.

video_title: The advice I wish someone told me as an engineering student
author: @Pabloe-58364
text:
I was similar to this, only in mechanical engineering. I graduated in the spring, but one thing I tell everybody is: if you have the chance during freshman and sophomore year, take summer school if you can.

I was not the smartest my freshman year—I almost dropped out and ended with a 2.7 GPA. In high school, I had a 4.0, was top of my class, and did robotics and athletics, but freshman year was hard because of the workload. I had no balance and ended up with a D in vector calculus and a C in basic physics.

During the summer, I started to learn how I study best and took core classes without a lot of distractions. It takes discipline, but if you do it, the difference between you and your classmates is insane—your brain gets stronger, you think quicker, and you have a much better understanding of the concepts.

The rest of my time at university, I made the Dean’s List, and senior year I ended with a 3.8 GPA. I got A’s in dynamics, fluids, and mechanics of materials. I truly think the summers were the most important part. Classes don’t last the full three months, so you still get some time off, but the time you put in prepares you for the next semesters.

After school, I’m working in defense, but I also spent a summer in Europe. Relax—you worked hard. Make connections with people. I’m still learning, and you should never think you know everything. Some days are hard, even in a dream job. I’ve worked at some of the world’s best aerospace companies, and I’m still learning. Take the time

author: @JoeSmith-jd5zg
text:
Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending to zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 30; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 500; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 1500 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

text:
I disagree with the "you don't need to understand the proofs and derivations"
The way I see it, proofs are a bit like understanding tools. Sure you know how to use it, but it's helpful to understand its ins and outs to know its limitations, where to apply them, and how to apply them. 
While I agree you don't need to sweat over the nuances of every line, engineers can benefit immensely from understanding proofs.

I'm a math teacher who is going back to school for mechanical engineering and my understanding of proofs helps out immensely in my statics class because there is so much trigonometry and line properties that I think many engineering students may find difficult to apply because they may not be versed in the why of their geometry.

author: @jaya7905
text: The odds were not against you. You took the very conventional route of doing internships in undergrad. That is how most people get their first engineering job in industry. Try getting a PhD and extensive knowledge in scientific research and then trying to get an entry-level, mid-level, or senior-level job as an engineer in industry. Your qualifications are way different than what they are looking for at all levels, so you get stuck in unstable, low-paying, hyper-competitive research jobs dependent on government funding and a small number of reviewers who may not understand or be into your proposals.

video_title: Advice for engineering students
author: @nileshkujurtrains
text:
Throw away the manufactured concepts like 'careers' and 'job titles'. The main purpose of life is to be a nobody and still living life to the fullest, with maxed out brain, body, and soul. Don't reduce your life into a CV. Live a life in such a way that you need to write a book in order to explain to others. The best way is to completely transform and evolve yourself into a self-taught superhuman polymath. Age doesn't matter. Use the internet especially shadow libraries like Anna's Archive and Library Genesis to self-educate, self-experiment, and expand ourselves on a variety of academic, creative, skills-based, business, political, social work, games, and athletic fields for life.
Humans, lets challenge ourselves to live a grand and epic life.

author: @맥스웰방정식-d5z
text: I feel often glad when I see other EE students or engineers, because I know that they’ve been through the same stuff I did. I recognize all those courses. I live in Sweden but the curriculums are almost the same everywhere. Calculus in one variable, multivariable analysis, linear algebra, programming, digital logic, physics 1 and 2, electrical engineering project, environmental engineering, circuit analysis, analog electronics, electromagnetism, signals & systems, measurement labs, probability & random process, semiconductor physics, control systems, communication systems, biomedical engineering, digital circuit labs. Currently I’m enrolled in my postgraduate program after undergrad (it’s a bachelor+master integrated program). I really wanna know how the work life looks. Sometimes I regret choosing this integrated program because the education is so long. But at the same time I’m also glad I got to learn all this knowledge that is fundamental in science and engineering.

text: I studied electrical engineering in the United States. We studied the same content. However the sequence that we have is different.  Here in the United States we have to complete all required math, physics and programming courses before we can take any electrical engineering courses. We begin with circuits and digital systems. Next we do electronics, electromagnetics, signals and systems, controls, electric machines probability, communications, power systems analysis courses,  engineeringeconomics. In our final year we had electives of electrical engineering specializations and team project to design and build, engineering ethics.

However, the ability to plan, derive, analyze, implement, test, verify, validate, deploy and support while maintaining adherence to a variety of standards matrixed to a development process for the various life cycles of a project is something only a software engineer can do. Coders simply don't have the skillset.

The fact that EE deals in digital design with literally transistors(Logical gates) can set up a deep knowledge of low level programming which can be used as ladder to high level programming languages. Also it provides knowledge in more core electronics disciplines. From another point of view, EE classes cointain more math than CS/SWE degree. Thats why I think can be a great set up for mastern in artifical intelligence, why also mastering embedded systems and electronics. I just see EE as great starting point to many tech EE-ECE-CS-SWE jobs. Knowing how to programm just alone is going to be replaced by AI, since it doesnt require that much logical analysis if you really just need to code something (design architecture of web app is different). Personally, If I had a software company and the 2 candidates would be equally good but one with EE degree and second with CS. I would probably go for EE candidate. My opinion

text:
Bad teachers and bad presentation of content

Math inherently is easy , the issue is we have teachers that think making thing overly complicated or get a hard on for the difficulty forget their job is to explain concepts Simply

Even in engineering school we should try understanding vs rig our.

Second this leads to the way math is presented , formulas only no real life applications , no beauty , no visuals.

It’s just bland kinda like a bowl of lukewarm porridge or oats ; for a kid or a student in college this just bores them to death instead of actually 

So yea you can be bad at math on your own cause your lazy and then you don’t put in the work to learn it or be curious. But it doesn’t help the math is ultimately displayed as boring and complicated when it single handlely effects every part of your life

The only thing a student can do is look at other resources apart from their school, delve into subjects they love and first get curious about math so they then learn it and find it uses
